Measured against a **completed migration** for the first time, and it changed
the answer.

A finished DeltaV system — 761 modules, built by hand from this same ABB project
— was read back against what the tool proposes from the export. Four things were
wrong, and all four are the kind that only a real answer sheet exposes.

**A tag is not a module.** `proposed_modules.csv` had one row per tagged block,
which sizes the job by an order of magnitude too high. The soft water tank level
is seven ABB tags — the measurement, a second range, the raw end, an alarm, a
latch and two edges — and **one** DeltaV module. A motor is its hour meters and
its run feedback as well; alarm limits (`-HA`, `-HiHi`, `-LA`) are parameters of
the measurement's module and not modules, and not one of the 470 such tags in
the real export exists as a module in the finished system. Rows are now one per
device, with the absorbed tags listed so nothing disappears quietly: 7,343
source tags resolve to 2,583 devices.

**The block types that matter most had no entry.** `IDF_1` is the plant device
block — motors, pumps, solenoid valves — 414 of them, and the legend had never
heard of it, so the tool reported the 414 most important tags

# v6

**Fixed: listing the registered OPC servers crashed the helper on machines that
have classic OPC installed.**

The helper asked Windows for the OPC server-list object, then used the answer as
if it were a different kind of object and called through it — an access violation
that killed it silently, with no message to show. It only happened where classic
OPC (OPCEnum) is actually registered: everywhere else the request fails first and
the tool correctly reported "no classic OPC here", which is why this went unseen.
It now asks for the interface it intends to use, matching what the rest of the
helper already did.

Connecting to a server, browsing, reading and writing tags were unaffected.

A frozen transmitter could be tuned as if it were a real response

Live logging read PV, OUT and SP with asyncua's `read_value()`, which returns the
value and throws the StatusCode away. A Bad, stale or frozen reading therefore
entered the dataset indistinguishable from live data — and a frozen transmitter
produces a clean, flat, entirely plausible response that the identifier fits
happily, handing back tuning constants for a loop that was never observed.

Reads now use the full DataValue and keep the quality:

- Logged samples carry a Quality flag (set when both PV and OUT came back Good).
  The status line warns the first time either goes not-good.
- Model fitting and the four-model competition refuse a window containing
  not-good samples, explaining why and asking before proceeding anyway.
- The step test aborts if OUT is not-good on the baseline read. Every step is
  measured against that number, so a bad baseline invalidates the whole test.
- CSV imports are taken at face value (Quality = good); the guard only ever
  fires on live-logged data.

- **32-bit binaries load at the right image base**, so addresses in the report

  that writes it, so files that previously could not be opened now can be.

# v6 (not yet built)
**`patina carchive` — read an undocumented MFC file format out of the binary
that writes it.** Aimed at the case where the binary is not the artefact you
care about: a proprietary document format with no schema.

- **The `CRuntimeClass` table** with each class's `sizeof`, its **archive
  schema**, and its base. The schema is the fact that matters and Patina was
  discarding it: a class whose schema is `0xFFFF` is `DECLARE_DYNAMIC`, so
  `CArchive` **never announces it by name** — a reader that expects every class
  to be tagged will mis-frame every record after the first.
- **The inlined `CArchive` fixed-width accessors**, with each one's **field
  width** and direction. Direction is decided by which side of the `mov` the
  archive buffer is on, not by anything sitting near it.

Validated against an independently hand-derived model of `GraphicsEd.dll`
(FactoryTalk View's graphics editor): 360 classes, and every checkable fact
agrees — `ZText` 504 bytes deriving from `ZUnrotatedRect`, `ZButtonElement` 3480
deriving from `ZPolygon`, the three `ZConnection*` classes alone at schema 1,
`ZDrawingElement`/`ZUnrotatedRect` both `DECLARE_DYNAMIC` and sharing one
`Serialize` at `0x6244ff90`. Generalises: RSLinx gives 198 classes and 4
primitives; a non-MFC binary reports nothing.

Two fixes made getting there, both of which affected existing behaviour:

- **`patina rtti` reported `[0 method(s)]` for every vtable in a 32-bit binary**
  while its own header claimed thousands — the slot walk used a hardcoded 8-byte
  stride. 1,980 of 1,980 wrong on one DLL, now 0.
- **Base-class recovery missed every shared-MFC (`_AFXDLL`) binary.** The getter
  is matched as the bytes `B8 imm32 C3`, but real builds emit it with a stack
  frame and behind a two-hop thunk. `carchive` decodes instead of byte-matching;
  `rtti`'s own walk still has the strict form.

# v5
Historian export comparator -- new `compare` CLI verb, no DeltaV connection needed

DvHistExport is no longer connection-only. `app.py` is now the built entry point
(`build.ps1`'s `-Entry "app"`): a `compare` verb on the command line runs headless,
before Tk or pythonnet/the DeltaV DLLs are even imported. No verb still opens the
window exactly as before, and `--selftest` is unchanged.

`DvHistExport.exe compare SOURCE.csv TARGET.csv --out REPORT.xlsx` compares two
historian exports (e.g. this tool's own "Export CSV..." output against a PI or
dataPARC export) for value/quality/timestamp agreement, matching samples within a
configurable time tolerance rather than requiring identical timestamps. It samples
`ceil(sqrt(N)) + 1` tags out of the total configured -- the same formula a real
Cornerstone dataPARC IQ/OQ deliverable uses to verify ongoing collection by hand
(72 of a 5000-tag system) -- chosen by even stride across the sorted tag list so
the sample is reproducible from the tag list alone. Writes a Sample Selection /
Comparison Evidence / Summary workbook. The comparison engine (`shared.histcompare`)
is shared with FHXport's new `historian-compare` verb, since neither side of a
historian-to-historian comparison is DeltaV-specific.

# v4
The quality column was inverted — every good sample was flagged bad

The sample list tested `status != 0` to decide whether to highlight a row. Quality
lives in the top two bits of the DeltaV status byte, so a good sample is 0x80–0xFF
and only 0x00 passed that test. The result was backwards: every GOODCASCADE and
GOODNONCASCADE sample was highlighted as bad, and the one genuinely bad byte
(0x00, BAD/non-specific) was shown as fine.

The status byte is now decoded through `shared.deltav.status` rather than guessed
at. Samples carry readable Quality, Substatus and Limit, the list highlights only
what is actually not-good, and the read summary says how many samples were not
good. The CSV export gains `quality`, `substatus`, `limit` and `is_good` columns
alongside the raw bytes, which are unchanged.

meanings are not yet documented.

## v6

- **Export any table to CSV.** The Discover, Device Explorer and Device Parameters
  tabs each gained an *Export to CSV* button. It writes the table exactly as shown
  — the visible columns, in order, with their heading text — to a CSV file you pick,
  so a discovered-device list, an object-model scan or a full parameter dump can go
  straight into a spreadsheet or a commissioning record. Output is UTF-8 with a BOM
  so Excel opens it without a mojibake prompt.

## v5

- **Probe now prefers the DPI object and reads cleanly on PowerFlex 520-series
  drives.** Validated against a real PowerFlex 525:
  - *Auto* now uses the DPI Parameter Object (0x93) when the device answers a full
    record — it returns name, units, min/max and scaling in one read (e.g.
    parameter 1 → name "Output Freq", units "Hz").
  - The standard Parameter Object (0x0F) fallback was hardened for the PF525's
    quirks: it recovers the parameter name when the drive returns it in the units
    attribute, and **infers the value type from its byte length** when the drive
    reports a non-standard type code — so values show as numbers instead of raw hex.
- Enumeration no longer depends on a working parameter-count read (walks until the
  device stops answering), and the object scan reports parameter-count correctly.

## v4

- **Device introspection — no PDF/EDS needed for most devices.** New *Device
  Explorer* tab plus a *Probe device* button on the parameters tab. The tool now
  asks the device to describe itself:
  - **Identity** — reads the Identity Object (0x01) for product name, revision,
    vendor/type/code, serial.
  - **Self-describing parameters** — walks the DPI Parameter Object (0x93) or the
    standard Parameter Object (0x0F) and reads each parameter's name, type, units,
    min/max/default and **scaling** straight from the device, so you get a live,
    named parameter list (with engineering-unit values) without an EDS. If an EDS
    *is* loaded it enriches the device data (help text, enum strings).
  - **Object-model scan** — probes the well-known CIP classes and shows which the
    device actually implements.
  - **EDS-off-device** (experimental) — uploads the device's own EDS via the File
    Object (0x37), the way Studio 5000/RSLinx do.
  - **Generic explicit-message poker** — send any service/class/instance/attribute
    and decode the reply, for anything the built-in views don't cover.
- **Fixed a second latent read bug:** responses were parsed from the start of the
  raw reply frame instead of the CIP data offset (byte 44). Values/IP config are now
  extracted correctly, and CIP error statuses are decoded to plain English.

## v3

- **Fixed "no parameters could be read" on drives/adapters.** Explicit-message
  reads and writes were being wrapped in an Unconnected_Send routed across a
  backplane to "slot 0" — correct for a ControlLogix chassis, but a standalone
  EtherNet/IP device (PowerFlex drive, EtherNet/IP adapter) has no backplane and
  rejects that route, so every read failed. The tool now sends bare UCMM explicit
  messages directly to the device, the way RSLogix and the drive AOP do.
- **Added the DPI Parameter Object (class 0x93)** used by PowerFlex 520-series
  drives (single read via attr 9; write to NVS via attr 9 or RAM-only via attr 10),
  alongside the generic Parameter Object (0x0F). The Device Parameters tab now has
  a **Parameter object** selector (Auto / DPI 0x93 / Standard 0x0F, default Auto,
  which tries DPI then falls back to 0x0F) and a **Write to** selector (NVS
  permanent / RAM-only temporary).

# v12

- **A find/replace no longer changes anything you did not ask it to.** Two defects
  fired on every FHX FnR wrote, with no rules involved at all — a read-then-save
  round trip was enough to reproduce both.
  - The UTF-16 byte-order mark was dropped. The reader stripped it and the writer
    never put it back, so every output was BOM-less UTF-16 — which is what DeltaV's
    FHX import reads as ANSI. Whether the source had one is now remembered and
    reproduced, rather than guessed at either way.
  - Line endings were rewritten. Both ends used default newline translation, so a
    lone CR came back as CRLF. Measured on the corpus: 8 of them, inside a `rem`
    block in an expression, adding 8 lines to every replicated file. Read and write
    are now byte-faithful, and a no-op round trip is byte-identical — pinned by a
    test, on a 3.6 MB real export as well as a fixture.

- **Composite named-set references are renamed on both sides.** `'_SET:VALUE'` was
  taken as one candidate. Both halves carry the unit suffix, a suffix transform
  rewrites only the trailing one, and because the composite is the longest find in
  the map it wins the span — so the correct rule for the set name, sitting right
  beside it, could never fire. The result was an expression referring to a named set
  that does not exist in the replicate: measured at 33 occurrences per file, in all
  five replicates. The reference is now split at the colon and each half gets its
  own rule.

  The general check matters more than the instance: no derived r

OperateTools.notes:
# v27

A rebuild; the tool itself behaves as described under v25.

- **No new behaviour in this release.** The pattern warnings, the "0 matches" explanations and the write-time checks described under v25 are all in this build.

# v25

- **Replacing a whole expression now works.** Collapsing an expression onto a single tag, re-shaping one
  (dropping some terms and adding others), and changing an `and` to an `or` where that changes the order the
  picture evaluates in — none of these could ever be written. Each was routed to an engine that built the
  edit, and a check at the very end refused it; because that check refuses the WHOLE picture, one awkward
  expression meant nothing in the file was written. Measured before: 0 of 8. Now every one of them applies,
  and the finished file is re-read to prove it.
  - The message you would have seen was *"N expression(s) would ship unreadable"* or *"N expression(s) would
    ship with N missing data-source connection(s)"*.
  - **No picture was ever damaged by this.** The refusal happened before anything was written. If a colleague
    ran Picture Repair on the file and it came back healthy, that was correct — the file was never the
    problem, the edit was. Both messages now say so.
  - Where a replacement needs a longer tag name than the picture has room for in that slot, that ONE
    expression is reported skipped with the reason, and the rest of the file is written as normal.
- **A new check that reads the finished picture before writing it.** Every earlier check inspected the edit
  in memory, and that is not the same thing as the file. An edit can look perfect in memory and still write a
  picture where fifteen expressions have operands with nothing driving them — the failure where an alarm
  colour reads correctly in the editor and simply never changes on screen. Every write is now re-read and its
  live-data connections compared against the original; if the edit made them worse, nothing is written.
- **"0 matches" now tells you WHY.** A pattern that finds nothing used to look identical whether
  the text is genuinely absent or the pattern is one clause away from right. The preview now
  works out how far the pattern DOES match and names the clause the picture stops agreeing with,
  with an example of the closest value it found. A 640-character alarm-colour pattern that
  reported nothing turned out to end in a `_CND_01/DEPRIORITIZE` clause that particular picture
  does not have — visible immediately now, where before it meant dumping every expression in the
  file by hand.
- **A replacement that DELETES tags now says which ones.** This is the quiet one. A greedy `(.*)`
  in the Find swallows whatever sits between the tokens you wrote, and if the replacement only
  writes `${1}` back, everything the wildcard ate is deleted. The rule looks like a rename and
  the preview row is 600 characters wide, so two alarm terms vanishing from the middle are
  invisible. Every preview row for an expression now names the tag references the rewrite would
  remove — whether it is applied or skipped.
  - Real case: a pattern naming `_TE_01`, `_TE_01B` and `_ZS_01` matched rooms that also read
    `_HT_01`, `_HT_01B` and `_ZS_02`, and would have dropped four of the five alarms each room
    monitors.
- **Removing a term from an expression now works.** It routed to the right engine and built the right token
  graph, but the shortened display string was moved in the process and the expression was left with no
  display text at all — so the whole-picture check refused the file. Every attempt to delete a term was
  refused; measured 0 of 6 before, 6 of 6 now. The display is rewritten in place, which is what the
  rename path has always done — both now share the one implementation.
- **The command-line tool now shows the same warnings as the GUI.** `operate-cli fr --regex`
  printed none of them: greedy wildcards, capture groups the replacement never reads, the
  `$1_TE_01` group-name trap, over-wide

## v13

DvScan now judges a system against the configuration it is actually running, not against every database the workstation has ever run.

- **The current configuration without an FHX.** The workstation's own device table (`download\DT.SCR`, the configuration as last downloaded) now counts as the configuration. Bindings for nodes it does not have are reported as **orphaned** without needing an FHX export.
- **Old databases stop looking like faults.** Nodes that only old POWERUP download images name are listed as **superseded**, greyed at the bottom, instead of "unreachable" or "conflicted". On LP1 the same system went from "2 conflicted, 16 unreachable" to "4 orphaned, 3 healthy, 13 superseded", and the four orphans were exactly the bindings to remove.
- **Remove binding for an I/O card's leftover.** A CIOC's identity lives in its I/O port, so DvScan never offered to touch its binding. When the binding names a node the configuration no longer has, it is this workstation's own stale file, and Remove binding is now offered for it.
- **Case file.** It now includes the current device table, lists superseded nodes in one compact table, and says so when DeltaV's Decommissioned Nodes list is empty.
- **Fixes.** A device-table conflict no longer shows an empty "claimed by more than one binding:" line, and long state labels such as "uncommissioned" are no longer clipped.

## v12

DvScan now reads what the ProPlus is doing as well as what is on its disk, and can carry out the fix it recommends.

- **Sees what coldStartServer is holding.** coldStartServer keeps the identity bindings it loaded at start-up and keeps pushing them after the .MAC file is deleted. # v6

A smaller, faster model, and it now runs whole on a 4 GB graphics card.

- **New model: Qwen3.5-4B.** It replaces Qwen2.5-Coder-7B. It is smaller (2.7 GB against 3.6 GB) and, on a 4 GB RTX 2050, answers at about 28 tokens a second where the old model managed 3-5. It was chosen by a test of four models on DeltaV Live questions. The suite's AI jobs were then run on both models with real project files (two inputs per job): the new model passed 19 where the old one passed 11, and timed out once where the old one timed out 18 times.
- **The whole model goes on the graphics card when it fits.** Before, a 4 GB card got 16 layers and the rest ran on the processor, which was the slow part. When the model does not fit, llama.cpp now decides how much goes on the card.
- **No hidden thinking.** The new model can think before it answers; the server turns that off, so tools get the answer straight away and JSON answers keep their shape.
- **Less memory.** The server kept up to 8 GB of old prompts in memory; it now keeps at most 512 MB.
- **A slow graphics-card check no longer puts the model on the processor.** If the check took more than 2 seconds, the server started with no layers on the card for the rest of the session.
- **The shipped model is chosen by name.** With more than one model in the models folder, the server used the first alphabetically.

# Doc2DV release notes

## Version 6

- **Tags drawn as letter outlines are read.** Some PDFs print a label as the outlines of its letters rather than as text. Doc2DV now reads those back into text, so the valve beside the label gets its tag. On the A3 screens that is seven more hand valves.
- **Small vessels stay whole, and apart.** A vessel whose label fills its body keeps its domes and flanges, and two vessels drawn near each other, or joined by a pipe drawn as a shape, are no longer made into one.
- **PCSD colour links for every shape.** On a PCSD job, a colour linked to a PCSD theme global (such as gs_pipe) now links rectangles, ovals, polygons, lines and the rest, not only texts, and those shapes follow the operator's theme in Run. Shapes inside a group keep their fixed colour for now.
- **Two instruments drawn as one shared-display pair** (such as FIC over FQI) are two symbols.
- **Command line:** `cli build --decisions` now applies the file's colours and links, as its help says, prints a `LINKS:` line, and reads a decisions file saved with a byte-order mark.
- All 23 A3 pages built with these changes open in DeltaV Operate on the pilot site node, and a PCSD page with theme links opens and runs on a PCSD node.

## Version 5

- **Builds with your site's own dynamo sets, not only PCSD's.** Doc2DV picks each symbol's dynamo by what the dynamo reads and what it is called, and learns from the site's own pictures which dynamo the site uses for each kind of device. A folder of dynamo sets is read as one set.
- **Dynamo samples made on the node.** "Make sample kit…" on the Build step writes a folder to take to the site's iFix node. There, iFix pastes each dynamo the pages use into a copy of the template, so the pictures carry what that node's own iFix writes. Every built page is checked against the samples, and a page that might not open on the node is flagged before it gets there.
- **Pages look like the site's own.** Given the site's pictures, Doc2DV reads the colours, line widths and fonts they use for each kind of thing (vessels, pipes, panels, tag boxes, labels, titles). Two buttons at the top of the Colours step, **Colour as site** and **Colour as PDF**, say where the colours come from, and each row shows whether its colour is the site's, the PDF's or your own pick. - **The page title goes in the template's title box.** The title box is resized so the whole title shows.
- **Vessels become the site's own tank parts.** Each vessel is matched to a site tank by its outline and stretched to fit, and the Symbols step shows the choice to keep or change.
- **Colours linked to the site's globals.** The new "Site globals" input takes the site's globals file (.fxg) or folder. On the Colours step, any colour can be linked to one of the site's colour globals, shown with its swatch and description, so the page follows the site's colour scheme in Run.

- **Values built from the tag.** In the Symbols step a dynamo variable can be given a typed value with `{tag}`, `{label}` or `{page}` in it, filled in for each copy: `DVSYS.{tag}` gives `DVSYS.XV-1001`, `{tag}/PV.CV` gives `XV-1001/PV.CV`.

# DataMask — release notes

## v1

First release of Mask Center, the data-protection mask's own window. It opens from the launcher's AI card ("🛡 Mask Center…"), from every tool's AI menu, or from its own tile.

- **What the mask does.** With Cloud AI masked chosen in a tool's AI menu, everything sent to a cloud AI has its customer names, sites, people, computer names, addresses and other free text replaced with stand-ins first, and the answer comes back with the real names. Words that are structure, ordinary English, DeltaV vocabulary or numbers stay readable, so the AI can still work (K360 becomes Q360, the same way every time). File structure stays valid: an FHX still parses, a Word or Excel file still opens.
- **Dictionary.** One per customer: names that must always be masked even when they are ordinary words, with their spellings and aliases, plus the never-masked words and domains. It can propose names from the project's files, the customer settings, DvVMManager's nodes and the RDP targets, for you to accept.
- **Vault.** The table of real names and their stand-ins for a customer. It stays on this PC, encrypted to your Windows login, and can be exported with a password to share with a colleague.
- **Preview.** Drop a file to see it masked side by side, with what changed highlighted and a check that nothing known was left.
- **Sanitized export.** A folder or zip in, a masked copy out (file names too), with a report of what was masked and anything it could not mask. For sending files to a vendor or support.
- **Logos, audit trail and policy.** Logos to paint over in images and PDFs; the per-project record of every cloud send; and the effective AI mode with the reason for it (a folder lock, a policy file or your choice).
